responses.strategic_rationale: This residential parasomnia unit navigates three intersecting tensions: capturing rare events (2–8 week stays yield events in ~70–80% of cases) while controlling cost and staff burnout, maintaining naturalistic behavior (domestic environment) while collecting clinical-grade data (tiered sensor acquisition), and scaling safely (8 active suites now, 12-suite capacity exists) without sacrificing participant safety or annotation throughput. The levers below address recruitment sustainability, event-capture efficiency, operational staffing models, data annotation scalability, facility utilization under resource constraints, regulatory compliance burden, and the fundamental trade-off between sensor burden and data quality — each lever directly impacts whether the unit achieves its 50–70 participant enrollment and minimum event-capture targets by month 36 within the €3.8M budget.

levers.name: Recruitment Flow and Participant Composition
levers.consequences: The ratio of self-reported event frequency (≥2 episodes per month is current threshold) to actual captured events determines both enrollment throughput and unproductive admissions. Tightening inclusion criteria (e.g., requiring ≥4 episodes per month) raises event-yield probability but narrows the population and slows recruitment; loosening criteria increases enrollment speed but inflates the 20% ceiling on zero-capture admissions, triggering protocol review. The stay-extension policy (up to 10 weeks total with two-week increments) extends bed occupancy for low-yield cases, competing directly with high-yield admissions.
options: Enforce pre-admission screening polysomnography or overnight actigraphy to confirm self-reported event frequency before enrollment, accepting a 4–8 week screening lag but reducing unproductive admissions below 15% and shortening average stays to 3–5 weeks.

Accept clinical interview and collateral history as sufficient without pre-admission monitoring, accepting higher initial unproductive rates (18–22%) but accelerating enrollment and relying on stay-extension protocol to recover phenotyping data from slow-yielding cases.

Stratify recruitment into a fast-track cohort (≥4 episodes per month, immediate admission) and standard-track cohort (2–4 episodes per month, queued with priority for stay-extension), balancing throughput with event-yield prediction and enabling real-time adjustment of the zero-capture ceiling.
levers.review_lever: Stricter pre-admission screening reduces unproductive admissions but adds recruitment latency and screening cost; looser criteria speed enrollment but risk overwhelming the stay-extension budget and creating a backlog of low-yield participants. All three options leave unaddressed how to handle borderline cases (self-reported episodes declining in frequency post-consent) that present after enrollment.

levers.name: Technician Annotation Throughput and Dual-Rater Reliability
levers.consequences: Each enhanced or escalation night generates 6–8 hours of PSG montage data requiring real-time technician flagging and later dual-rater scoring; at 30–35 admissions per year (year two target) with an average of 2–3 scored nights per stay, the team faces 60–105 nights requiring dual-rater annotation. Technician fatigue during night shifts degrades real-time event detection sensitivity; inter-rater reliability (target unreported but typically 0.75–0.85 kappa) requires extensive training and calibration time. Outsourcing scoring to external raters reduces technician load but introduces cost and latency; in-house dual-scoring by the same technician pair risks correlated bias.
options: Hire two additional part-time independent scorers (e.g., trained sleep technicians or neurophysiology graduates) on per-night contract basis, compensating them for dual-rater annotation at €150–200 per night, freeing night technicians to focus on real-time detection and participant safety while establishing blinded dual scoring.

Establish a scoring protocol requiring all enhanced and escalation nights to be scored in tandem by the night technician and the postdoctoral neurophysiology researcher within 48 hours post-shift, with discrepancies resolved by the PI, embedding scoring into the existing payroll structure but risking postdoc burnout if event rates exceed 2 per week.

Develop a semi-automated preliminary event-triage tool (feeding low-burden sensor streams into rule-based detection, not autonomous diagnosis) that flags candidate events with confidence scores, reducing the dual-rater pool to only flagged-and-high-confidence events while using technician-only review for low-confidence candidates, accepting lower sensitivity on borderline events.
levers.review_lever: In-house dual-scoring preserves blinding and control but creates staff bottlenecks; outsourcing adds cost and coordination overhead. All three options sidestep the threshold question of what inter-rater kappa target justifies reporting Aim 2 phenotyping claims.

levers.name: Facility Expansion Timeline and Bed Utilization
levers.consequences: Eight active suites with a 70–80% event-capture rate and 2–8 week average stays implies 6–8 admissions per month at steady state; at 30–35 participants per year (year two target), the unit operates at approximately 85% occupancy if stays average 3 weeks. Expanding to 12 suites increases capacity but requires additional renovation cost, electrical load management in the leased property, 1–2 extra night technicians for safe coverage (night shifts require ≥1 technician per 4–5 suites), and risk of underutilization if recruitment stalls. Deferring expansion to year two or three preserves capital but risks losing high-yield participants to referral delays and reduces publication readiness by narrowing the phenotyping sample.
options: Proceed with 12-suite buildout in year one (additional €400–500K capital and 1–2 FTE technician hires), absorbing the construction timeline and upfront cost but reaching full capacity by month 12 and positioning for 50–70 enrollments by month 24.

Maintain 8 active suites through year two, monitoring recruitment and event-capture metrics monthly, and trigger a 12-suite expansion decision at month 18 only if monthly admission rate exceeds 3 participants and stays average <3 weeks, deferring €400K capital until utilization is proven.

Implement a dynamic two-cohort model: maintain 8 suites for 2–8 week longitudinal admissions (standard protocol) and dedicate 2 additional suites for 3-night diagnostic immersions (first night PSG, follow-up night, discharge), capturing event data from referrals unable to commit to longer stays and increasing annual throughput without full 12-suite infrastructure.
levers.review_lever: Early expansion risks overcapacity and wasted staffing; delayed expansion risks recruitment backlog and publication delays. None of the options quantify the break-even occupancy rate at which 12-suite marginal cost per participant falls below €8K.

levers.name: Night-Shift Staffing Model and Safety Coverage
levers.consequences: Safe coverage of 8 suites with event response, participant welfare checks, and real-time annotation requires rotating shifts covering approximately 10.5 hours per night (20:00–06:30), equaling 3.5 full-time night technician positions (accounting for German statutory rest days and sick leave). Current budget of €2M personnel costs over three years supports this core team plus day staff; each additional technician adds €80–100K annually in gross salary and benefits. Inadequate night staffing risks delayed event response (physiological safety during sleepwalking or terror escalation), incomplete real-time annotation (flagged events missed), and technician burnout (six consecutive nights erodes alertness). Shift schedules also affect local recruitment (night workers must live within 30 minutes of Bonn).
options: Employ three full-time night technicians on permanent 10.5-hour rotating schedules, ensuring no single technician works more than 2 consecutive nights and maintaining one technician per 2.5–3 suites for both safety and annotation capacity, accepting the fixed-cost overhead regardless of occupancy.

Contract with a professional medical staffing agency (e.g., Pflege-Plus or equivalent in Bonn) to supply on-call night technicians on a per-shift basis (€80–120 per shift), scaling staffing with occupancy, but accepting loss of continuity, potential knowledge gaps in sensor troubleshooting, and ~2-week recruitment lag if sudden illness reduces agency availability.

Establish a hybrid model: employ 2 full-time core night technicians (ensuring continuity and deep system knowledge) plus 1–2 part-time evening technicians (18:00–00:00) to handle early-shift event annotation and participant settling, allowing the core team to focus on midnight–06:30 response and reducing consecutive-night exposure.
levers.review_lever: Full-time permanent staffing guarantees safety and consistency but locks in fixed wages even during low-occupancy periods (risk in year one). Agency staffing cuts fixed costs but introduces continuity gaps and knowledge loss during critical event-response moments. All options underspecify the protocol for technician incident reporting and PI escalation during events.

levers.name: Sensor Acquisition Burden and Data Quality Trade-off
levers.consequences: The tiered model (low-burden nightly monitoring plus scheduled enhanced PSG nights) balances ecological validity with clinical-grade data, but nightly dry-electrode EEG headbands, mattress sensors, and infrared cameras generate substantial false-positive triggers (movement, arousal, position changes) unrelated to parasomnia events. Increasing sensor frequency (e.g., full PSG every night) yields richer data but raises participant burden, amplifies comfort concerns that suppress naturalistic behavior, and increases technician time per night. Reducing sensors (e.g., nightly EEG headband only) preserves naturalism but weakens event confidence during the scheduled enhanced nights because you lack baseline physiological reference.
options: Deploy full PSG montage (scalp EEG, EOG, EMG) on all study nights for all participants, trading ecological validity for clinical-grade capture of every potential event and eliminating the need for enhanced-night escalations, but projecting 15–20% higher dropout rates due to electrode discomfort and 30% increase in night-technician annotation time.

Retain the current tiered model (dry EEG headband nightly, full PSG on first, mid, and final nights) and invest 3 months in training two independent raters to distinguish artifact and incidental movement from true parasomnia events, using standardized video-plus-EEG review criteria, reducing false-positive burden without increasing participant burden.

Implement a participant-feedback loop: after each night, present raw sensor flags and video clips to participants with a simple questionnaire ("Did you experience an episode? Describe it."), using collateral self-report to pre-filter technician annotation targets and focusing dual-rater effort on events participants self-confirm, trading some missed events for marked reduction in false-positive review burden.
levers.review_lever: Full PSG every night maximizes data integrity but risks ecological validity and higher dropout; tiered with training requires rater consistency investment but does not address the fundamental sensitivity-specificity trade-off in distinguishing parasomnia from normal sleep movement. The feedback-loop option introduces recall bias and may suppress naturalism if participants feel evaluated.

levers.name: Regulatory and Ethics Compliance Pathway
levers.consequences: Initial ethics approval (expected 8–12 weeks from submission) is a hard dependency for enrollment; expansion to RBD under a separate protocol (as planned) requires a second ethics amendment and potentially a separate IRB review cycle, adding 4–8 weeks and delaying RBD recruitment into year two. Secondary analyses (e.g., leveraging the physiological dataset for unexpected correlates) may trigger post-hoc approval requests, especially if external collaborators request data outside the original data-use scope. Annual ethics renewals and safety reports (incident reporting from the facility) are mandatory in Germany (Ethikkommission der Medizinischen Fakultät, Universität Bonn) and typically require 2–4 weeks turnaround.
options: Submit the primary NREM protocol and RBD protocol as a single integrated ethics application with a clear separation-of-concerns design (distinct inclusion criteria, distinct safety triggers, distinct data-sharing scopes), requesting approval for both arms simultaneously and targeting a single ethics committee review cycle of 10–12 weeks, accepting the risk that committee questions on one arm delay both.

Secure primary ethics approval for the NREM-only protocol (8–10 weeks) and launch enrollment immediately, then file the RBD amendment as a separate protocol after 6 months of NREM operational data, positioning the RBD arm as a secondary expansion with approval expected by month 14, accepting a staggered recruitment timeline but reducing upfront approval risk.

Engage a regulatory consultant (€5–10K one-time fee) specializing in German multi-site sleep research to pre-screen the protocol for ethics feasibility, prepare a comprehensive safety monitoring plan and incident-reporting template, and draft the RBD amendment in parallel with NREM enrollment, aiming to submit both protocols simultaneously after month 3 and avoiding re-work delays.
levers.review_lever: Bundled approval reduces total timeline but concentrates risk on a single committee decision; staggered approval isolates NREM launch but delays RBD recruitment. Consultant involvement adds cost but does not guarantee committee acceptance or shorter turnaround if the committee requests major protocol revisions.

levers.name: Data Sharing and Publication Strategy
levers.consequences: The plan restricts public deposition of video data (privacy constraints) but commits to de-identified physiological data in a recognized repository (e.g., openneuro.org or PhysioNet), enabling reproducibility and external validation of event-triage algorithms. However, de-identifying polysomnography and sensor data while preserving clinical utility requires careful balancing: removing timestamps and demographic details limits secondary-use machine-learning; retaining sufficient metadata (age ranges, time-of-night clustering, seasonal pattern) aids methodology validation but raises re-identification risk. First-mover publication pressure (2–3 papers by month 36) competes with data-release timing: data-sharing pipelines require 2–3 months of post-collection curation and de-identification review, potentially delaying publication if the same dataset is submitted for curation before peer-review acceptance.
options: Publish methods and initial cohort phenotyping (Aim 2 results) by month 24 using a locked dataset of the first 20–25 participants, then curate and deposit the full de-identified dataset (month 26–28) after publications are accepted, maximizing priority and controlling narrative, but delaying reproducibility claims until 6 months after publication.

Conduct publication and data curation in parallel: submit Aim 2 phenotyping manuscript by month 22, begin de-identification and repository submission by month 23, and commit to data release within 2 months of manuscript acceptance, accepting a tighter timeline and potential minor delays if reviewer feedback requires additional cohort analysis before data lock.

Establish a formal data-sharing partnership with one external sleep research group (e.g., Max Planck Institute for Human Development or a Swiss sleep center) to conduct Aim 3 event-triage algorithm development on the dataset under a data-use agreement, positioning the external collaborators as co-authors on the methods and algorithm paper, distributing publication load and potentially improving algorithm robustness through external validation.
levers.review_lever: Early publication prioritizes scientific priority but delays reproducibility; parallel curation adds timeline pressure and risks incomplete de-identification if dataset changes are needed post-publication. External collaboration builds validation credibility but introduces coordination overhead and potential authorship disputes if the partner pursues independent analyses.

responses.strategic_rationale: This early-stage residential parasomnias research facility faces three core tensions: (1) balancing naturalistic home-like environment against clinical safety and monitoring capability, (2) capturing rare episodic events reliably while managing false-alarm annotation burden and inter-rater reliability, and (3) sustaining operational continuity and participant safety with a lean 9-person team across 8 suites operating 24/7. The levers below address scheduling and shift resilience, sensor deployment economics and false-positive mitigation, control-group strategy and phenotyping scope, data retention and regulatory risk, publication sequencing and funder narrative, equipment lifecycle and budget flexibility, and team skill composition during early operations—each reveals a distinct trade-off between scientific rigor, operational sustainability, and financial runway.

levers.name: Night-Shift Staffing Rotation and Coverage Continuity
levers.consequences: A rigid three-technician rotation covering 8 suites every night provides immediate incident response but locks in wage costs regardless of occupancy or absence. Conversely, a flexible on-call model with weekend-only overlap reduces fixed overhead but introduces delayed response times during peak event nights and increases burnout risk for the two full-time technicians, degrading annotation quality and inter-rater reliability over the first 18 months.
options: Hire a fourth part-time overnight technician on a split-shift schedule (21:00–02:00 and 02:00–07:00) to provide dedicated overlap coverage during the statistically busiest event hours, accepting the 20% wage increase in exchange for reduced response latency and annotation fatigue.

Maintain the original three-technician rotation but introduce a per-suite silent alarm escalation protocol that wakes the PI on call and a second technician from adjacent suites when motion or audio triggers exceed threshold, enabling coordinated response without a fourth body.

Stagger participant admissions so that no more than 6 of 8 suites are occupied simultaneously during the first 12 months, leaving capacity to absorb sick leave and vacation without hiring additional night staff, then reassess staffing ratios once operational baseline data validates safe suite-to-technician ratios.
levers.review_lever: Three technicians covering 8 suites nightly creates fatigue-driven annotation errors that feed inter-rater disagreement; none of these options directly address seasonal or pandemic-driven absence surges that might force temporary closure.

levers.name: Dry-Electrode Headband Signal Quality Thresholding and False-Alarm Reduction
levers.consequences: Setting a permissive EEG signal-quality threshold on the nightly headband captures more candidate events but floods the annotation queue with motion artifact and respiration noise, requiring the technician and two independent scorers to dismiss dozens of non-events per week. Raising the threshold reduces false positives but risks missing low-amplitude confusional arousals and subtle leg-movement episodes, biasing the phenotype toward higher-amplitude events and introducing selection artifact into Aim 2 longitudinal characterization.
options: Deploy a rolling 48-hour sensor calibration phase for each participant using the first two headband nights to establish individual signal-quality baselines, then apply person-specific thresholds that account for electrode impedance drift and scalp conductivity variation, reducing false alarms by 30–40% without raising the absolute threshold.

Implement a two-tier annotation workflow: technician performs rapid triage flagging only high-confidence motor clusters in the first pass, then dual scorers review only flagged segments plus a random 15% sample of low-confidence segments, trading marginal sensitivity loss for a 50% reduction in dual-rater review time and fatigue.

Accept the false-alarm burden as a necessary cost of sensitivity during the pilot phase, logging all headband detections and final adjudication outcomes, then conduct a post-hoc analysis at month 12 to derive data-driven thresholds that maximize sensitivity and specificity against the accumulated ground truth of dual-scorer consensus events.
levers.review_lever: Headband-derived false alarms drive annotation bottleneck and rater fatigue, but none of these options address inter-rater disagreement on borderline motor episodes when the true event morphology is genuinely ambiguous rather than artifact.

levers.name: Matched Control Recruitment Scope and Phenotyping Complexity
levers.consequences: Enrolling a 1:1 matched control group (15–20 controls alongside 50–70 parasomnias participants) provides definitive baseline sensor false-positive rates and normal nocturnal movement patterns for benchmarking event-triage tools, but doubles participant recruitment burden and adds ~8–10 weeks of facility occupancy during year one and two. A smaller control cohort (n=8–10) enrolled once and measured longitudinally reduces recruitment overhead but yields less statistical power for sensor-specificity claims and may not generalize across seasons or age subgroups.
options: Recruit and monitor 15 age-matched and sex-matched controls during year one in a dedicated 2-week intensive block, then retest a 50% subsample in year three to quantify seasonal variation in baseline arousal and movement; this front-loads control acquisition but yields robust phenotypic anchoring for Aim 2 analyses.

Enroll controls opportunistically from the University Hospital Bonn sleep clinic screening pool and the Deutsche Gesellschaft für Schlafforschung und Schlafmedizin network, recruiting 5–7 controls per quarter rather than in a block, spreading acquisition cost across 18 months but accepting lower matching fidelity and increased logistical complexity.

Defer formal matched control enrollment and instead use the first 10–12 parasomnias participants as their own pre-admission baseline: conduct one 3-night monitoring run before diagnostic confirmation, then enroll for treatment as usual; controls become unnecessary if cross-individual event-free nights sufficiently characterize sensor false-positive profiles, reducing recruitment pressure but weakening the generalizability of benchmarking data.
levers.review_lever: Matched controls anchor event-triage benchmarking but require recruitment parity with patients, straining capacity during year one; none of these options distinguish between healthy young controls and age-representative normal sleepers, so specificity claims remain limited to the cohort composition.

levers.name: Data Retention Timeline and Regulatory Burden Trade-off
levers.consequences: Retaining raw sensor streams (EEG, video, audio, mattress, infrared) for the full 5-year standard research data archival period ensures full auditability and enables future reanalysis, but multiplies storage costs, privacy-compliance overhead, and legal liability if de-identification fails or a participant later objects to bedroom video retention. Purging raw video and audio after 12 months of phenotyping and event adjudication reduces privacy risk and storage burden by approximately 60% but forecloses future computer-vision or acoustic reanalysis and creates ambiguity about what "de-identified" video actually means under German data protection law.
options: Implement a tiered retention policy: keep raw EEG, contact-free sensors (mattress, infrared motion), and metadata indefinitely; delete all bedroom audio and video within 90 days of final event adjudication, storing only time-stamped motion-onset coordinates and expert-annotated event descriptions, minimizing privacy liability while preserving physiological reanalysis capability.

Secure explicit informed consent during recruitment specifically permitting 10-year video retention in a locked archive accessible only to the PI and independent ethics oversight; store video and audio on air-gapped encrypted drives in the university legal office, not on research NAS, creating institutional separation between clinical data and video materials and reducing hacking surface area.

Adopt a strict 12-month purge schedule for all raw sensory data (video, audio, mattress sensor waveforms) immediately following independent dual-score event adjudication and publication-related reanalysis, retaining only summary-level event timing, morphology codes, and EEG spectrograms, meeting German data minimization principles and reducing regulatory risk at the cost of forfeiting raw-signal reanalysis optionality.
levers.review_lever: Video retention creates privacy and legal exposure proportional to duration, but deletion prevents future reanalysis; none of these options address the ambiguity of whether time-stamped motion coordinates alone constitute de-identification under GDPR if behavioral patterns are individually identifiable.

levers.name: Publication Sequencing and Funder Narrative Continuity
levers.consequences: Publishing the methods-validation and Aim 1 operational results first (month 18–20) establishes credibility with DFG and University of Bonn for year three funding but requires delaying high-impact Aim 2 phenotyping results until month 24–28, potentially ceding narrative momentum and allowing competitors to publish similar longitudinal characterizations. Publishing Aim 2 findings first (month 22–24) captures novelty but risks methods-validation criticism and may limit acceptance in top-tier journals if operational sustainability is not yet proven, weakening renewal justification.
options: Sequence publications as a dual-track strategy: submit the operational and inter-rater reliability methods paper to a sleep medicine journal at month 18, simultaneously developing a preprint of preliminary Aim 2 phenotype findings at month 20, allowing the phenotyping narrative to circulate while the peer-review process validates methods credibility, reducing journal competition pressure.

Prioritize a single high-visibility integrated publication at month 24 that binds methods validation (Aim 1) and preliminary longitudinal phenotyping (Aim 2) results in a unified narrative, leveraging the combined dataset and operational proof of concept to argue for continuation funding, accepting slower initial publication pace in exchange for coherence and impact.

Publish early and frequently: release operational and safety findings at month 12 as a short technical brief, then roll out Aim 2 phenotypic results in a series of three focused papers (one per parasomnia type) between months 20–28, building publication momentum and demonstrating sustained productivity to funder panels, but accepting fragmentation of the research narrative across multiple venues.
levers.review_lever: Early publication establishes funder confidence but fragmented output dilutes narrative impact; deferring publication until Aim 2 solidifies scientific novelty but delays interim reporting that funders expect by month 18, risking conditional-year-three funding review.

levers.name: Equipment Lifecycle and Budget Flexibility Under Vendor Obsolescence
levers.consequences: Purchasing all sensor hardware and PSG equipment outright in year one (€450K budget) provides immediate availability and no recurring licensing fees but locks capital into gear with 3–5 year hardware lifecycles, risking obsolescence of dry-electrode headband technology or mattress sensors if competitors release materially superior designs by year two. Leasing or renting core PSG equipment spreads costs across years but introduces vendor lock-in, recurring annual fees (~€80–120K estimated), and potential service discontinuation if the rental provider exits the market.
options: Commit to purchasing the core PSG equipment and dry-electrode headbands outright in year one, then establish a technology-refresh contingency fund (€50–80K) in year two budgets to upgrade or replace underperforming sensors if benchmarking data (month 12) reveals false-alarm or signal-quality deficits, accepting some capital waste in exchange for flexibility and avoiding multi-year rental contracts.

Lease all non-permanent equipment (PSG amplifiers, dry-electrode headbands, camera and infrared hardware) on 24-month renewable agreements with the major manufacturers, treating equipment as operational expenses rather than capital, freeing budget for participant compensation and scoring labor but committing to €30K annual recurring costs and potential service interruptions.

Negotiate a volume-discount research partnership with the primary sensor vendors (Emotiv or comparable dry-EEG provider, Beddit or equivalent for mattress sensing) offering free or deeply discounted equipment in year one in exchange for publication acknowledgment and de-identified aggregate benchmarking data, deferring €100–150K in upfront equipment costs to year two conditional on partnership approval.
levers.review_lever: Outright purchase locks capital and risk into hardware lifecycles; leasing spreads cost but creates vendor dependency; neither option hedges against fundamental sensor-technology disruption (e.g., transition from dry-electrode to textile-integrated sensing) without explicit contingency rebudgeting.

levers.name: Core Team Skill Composition and Operational Dependency Risk
levers.consequences: Hiring two postdoctoral researchers with PhDs in sleep neurophysiology and computational neuroscience (per the current staffing plan) ensures deep domain expertise for algorithm development and Aim 3 triage-tool benchmarking, but both roles are typically 2–3 year appointments, creating turnover risk and knowledge loss if either postdoc departs before month 18. Alternatively, hiring a single mid-career research scientist (MSc-level, 5+ years sleep lab experience) paired with a junior computational analyst reduces domain depth and limits Aim 3 algorithm sophistication but provides stability and lower salary drag, freeing €80–120K for participant compensation or technician support over three years.
options: Recruit the two postdoctoral researchers as planned, but negotiate explicit co-mentorship and cross-training protocols: the sleep neurophysiology postdoc mentors one research technician in semi-automated event detection during months 6–12, and the computational postdoc documents all algorithm development in a shared GitHub repository with comprehensive annotations, ensuring operational continuity if either postdoc departs by year three.

Hire a single tenured or indefinite-contract research scientist (sleep neurophysiology background, age 40–55) alongside one full-time junior data analyst, accepting reduced cutting-edge algorithmic ambition for Aim 3 but gaining institutional memory, willingness to supervise technicians long-term, and lower turnover risk, reallocating €50K from salaries to technician peer-support training and participant incentives.

Maintain the two-postdoc structure but add a commitment to co-author agreements requiring collaborative publication during the second postdoc's final year and a mandatory 3-month knowledge-transition period before departure; simultaneously hire a third part-time graduate-student research assistant (10 h/wk) to shadow both postdocs and build algorithmic literacy, creating a tiered skill buffer against mid-career departures.
levers.review_lever: Two postdocs provide algorithmic depth but 2–3 year appointments create continuity risk; none of these options directly address recruitment difficulty for specialized postdoctoral talent in smaller research markets like Bonn, potentially extending hiring timelines by 2–4 months and delaying project start.

levers.name: Exclusion Criteria Adjudication and Recruitment Velocity Trade-off
levers.consequences: Strict pre-admission adjudication (specialist clinical interview, bed-partner collateral, prior polysomnography, structured exclusion checklist) minimizes misdiagnosis and excludes mimics (nocturnal epilepsy, uncontrolled apnea, psychiatric instability) but requires 4–6 weeks of vetting per referral, reducing recruitment velocity to 4–6 participants per quarter and risking enrollment shortfall during year one if referral channels are slow to establish. Streamlined screening (telephone symptom checklist plus one polysomnography session) accelerates admission to 10–12 participants per quarter but risks enrolling atypical cases (ambiguous epilepsy-parasomnia overlap, subclinical apnea) that distort phenotyping and increase false-event rates.
options: Implement a two-stage filtering process: rapid telephone triage (30 min) by a trained sleep coordinator eliminates obvious exclusions (untreated epilepsy, active substance use), then schedule in-person PI interview and prior polysomnography review only for screened-positive candidates, reducing vetting time to 2–3 weeks and achieving 8–10 quarterly admissions without loosening exclusion precision.

Establish a standing weekly "diagnostic case conference" with the PI, clinical psychologist, and a collaborating neurologist from the University Hospital Bonn epilepsy service, where borderline referrals (possible nocturnal seizures, RBD-parasomnia overlap) are discussed before rejection, creating a second-opinion buffer that converts 15–20% of otherwise-excluded cases into admitted participants with documented adjudication rationale.

Maintain strict pre-admission criteria (specialist interview, collateral, prior PSG, structured checklist) and use slow initial recruitment to validate the diagnostic pipeline thoroughly, accepting lower year-one enrollment (12–15 participants) but building operational confidence and reducing mid-study protocol deviations, then scale recruitment aggressively in year two once the vetting process is proven robust.
levers.review_lever: Strict pre-admission screening ensures phenotypic homogeneity but delays recruitment; rapid screening accelerates admissions but introduces diagnostic ambiguity; none of these options address the limited availability of prior polysomnography in referred cases, which may force real-time diagnostic screening polysomnography during the facility stay rather than pre-admission.

levers.review: Early expansion risks overcapacity and wasted staffing; delayed expansion risks recruitment backlog and publication delays. None of the options quantify the break-even occupancy rate at which 12-suite marginal cost per participant falls below €8K.

levers.name: Night-Shift Staffing Model and Safety Coverage
levers.consequences: Safe coverage of 8 suites with event response, participant welfare checks, and real-time annotation requires rotating shifts covering approximately 10.5 hours per night (20:00–06:30), equaling 3.5 full-time night technician positions (accounting for German statutory rest days and sick leave). Current budget of €2M personnel costs over three years supports this core team plus day staff; each additional technician adds €80–100K annually in gross salary and benefits. Inadequate night staffing risks delayed event response (physiological safety during sleepwalking or terror escalation), incomplete real-time annotation (flagged events missed), and technician burnout (six consecutive nights erodes alertness). Shift schedules also affect local recruitment (night workers must live within 30 minutes of Bonn).
options: Employ three full-time night technicians on permanent 10.5-hour rotating schedules, ensuring no single technician works more than 2 consecutive nights and maintaining one technician per 2.5–3 suites for both safety and annotation capacity, accepting the fixed-cost overhead regardless of occupancy.

Contract with a professional medical staffing agency (e.g., Pflege-Plus or equivalent in Bonn) to supply on-call night technicians on a per-shift basis (€80–120 per shift), scaling staffing with occupancy, but accepting loss of continuity, potential knowledge gaps in sensor troubleshooting, and ~2-week recruitment lag if sudden illness reduces agency availability.

Establish a hybrid model: employ 2 full-time core night technicians (ensuring continuity and deep system knowledge) plus 1–2 part-time evening technicians (18:00–00:00) to handle early-shift event annotation and participant settling, allowing the core team to focus on midnight–06:30 response and reducing consecutive-night exposure.
levers.review: Full-time permanent staffing guarantees safety and consistency but locks in fixed wages even during low-occupancy periods (risk in year one). Agency staffing cuts fixed costs but introduces continuity gaps and knowledge loss during critical event-response moments. All options underspecify the protocol for technician incident reporting and PI escalation during events.

levers.name: Sensor Acquisition Burden and Data Quality Trade-off
levers.consequences: The tiered model (low-burden nightly monitoring plus scheduled enhanced PSG nights) balances ecological validity with clinical-grade data, but nightly dry-electrode EEG headbands, mattress sensors, and infrared cameras generate substantial false-positive triggers (movement, arousal, position changes) unrelated to parasomnia events. Increasing sensor frequency (e.g., full PSG every night) yields richer data but raises participant burden, amplifies comfort concerns that suppress naturalistic behavior, and increases technician time per night. Reducing sensors (e.g., nightly EEG headband only) preserves naturalism but weakens event confidence during the scheduled enhanced nights because you lack baseline physiological reference.
options: Deploy full PSG montage (scalp EEG, EOG, EMG) on all study nights for all participants, trading ecological validity for clinical-grade capture of every potential event and eliminating the need for enhanced-night escalations, but projecting 15–20% higher dropout rates due to electrode discomfort and 30% increase in night-technician annotation time.

Retain the current tiered model (dry EEG headband nightly, full PSG on first, mid, and final nights) and invest 3 months in training two independent raters to distinguish artifact and incidental movement from true parasomnia events, using standardized video-plus-EEG review criteria, reducing false-positive burden without increasing participant burden.

Implement a participant-feedback loop: after each night, present raw sensor flags and video clips to participants with a simple questionnaire ("Did you experience an episode? Describe it."), using collateral self-report to pre-filter technician annotation targets and focusing dual-rater effort on events participants self-confirm, trading some missed events for marked reduction in false-positive review burden.
levers.review: Full PSG every night maximizes data integrity but risks ecological validity and higher dropout; tiered with training requires rater consistency investment but does not address the fundamental sensitivity-specificity trade-off in distinguishing parasomnia from normal sleep movement. The feedback-loop option introduces recall bias and may suppress naturalism if participants feel evaluated.

levers.name: Regulatory and Ethics Compliance Pathway
levers.consequences: Initial ethics approval (expected 8–12 weeks from submission) is a hard dependency for enrollment; expansion to RBD under a separate protocol (as planned) requires a second ethics amendment and potentially a separate IRB review cycle, adding 4–8 weeks and delaying RBD recruitment into year two. Secondary analyses (e.g., leveraging the physiological dataset for unexpected correlates) may trigger post-hoc approval requests, especially if external collaborators request data outside the original data-use scope. Annual ethics renewals and safety reports (incident reporting from the facility) are mandatory in Germany (Ethikkommission der Medizinischen Fakultät, Universität Bonn) and typically require 2–4 weeks turnaround.
options: Submit the primary NREM protocol and RBD protocol as a single integrated ethics application with a clear separation-of-concerns design (distinct inclusion criteria, distinct safety triggers, distinct data-sharing scopes), requesting approval for both arms simultaneously and targeting a single ethics committee review cycle of 10–12 weeks, accepting the risk that committee questions on one arm delay both.

Secure primary ethics approval for the NREM-only protocol (8–10 weeks) and launch enrollment immediately, then file the RBD amendment as a separate protocol after 6 months of NREM operational data, positioning the RBD arm as a secondary expansion with approval expected by month 14, accepting a staggered recruitment timeline but reducing upfront approval risk.

Engage a regulatory consultant (€5–10K one-time fee) specializing in German multi-site sleep research to pre-screen the protocol for ethics feasibility, prepare a comprehensive safety monitoring plan and incident-reporting template, and draft the RBD amendment in parallel with NREM enrollment, aiming to submit both protocols simultaneously after month 3 and avoiding re-work delays.
levers.review: Bundled approval reduces total timeline but concentrates risk on a single committee decision; staggered approval isolates NREM launch but delays RBD recruitment. Consultant involvement adds cost but does not guarantee committee acceptance or shorter turnaround if the committee requests major protocol revisions.

levers.name: Data Sharing and Publication Strategy
levers.consequences: The plan restricts public deposition of video data (privacy constraints) but commits to de-identified physiological data in a recognized repository (e.g., openneuro.org or PhysioNet), enabling reproducibility and external validation of event-triage algorithms. However, de-identifying polysomnography and sensor data while preserving clinical utility requires careful balancing: removing timestamps and demographic details limits secondary-use machine-learning; retaining sufficient metadata (age ranges, time-of-night clustering, seasonal pattern) aids methodology validation but raises re-identification risk. First-mover publication pressure (2–3 papers by month 36) competes with data-release timing: data-sharing pipelines require 2–3 months of post-collection curation and de-identification review, potentially delaying publication if the same dataset is submitted for curation before peer-review acceptance.
options: Publish methods and initial cohort phenotyping (Aim 2 results) by month 24 using a locked dataset of the first 20–25 participants, then curate and deposit the full de-identified dataset (month 26–28) after publications are accepted, maximizing priority and controlling narrative, but delaying reproducibility claims until 6 months after publication.

Conduct publication and data curation in parallel: submit Aim 2 phenotyping manuscript by month 22, begin de-identification and repository submission by month 23, and commit to data release within 2 months of manuscript acceptance, accepting a tighter timeline and potential minor delays if reviewer feedback requires additional cohort analysis before data lock.

Establish a formal data-sharing partnership with one external sleep research group (e.g., Max Planck Institute for Human Development or a Swiss sleep center) to conduct Aim 3 event-triage algorithm development on the dataset under a data-use agreement, positioning the external collaborators as co-authors on the methods and algorithm paper, distributing publication load and potentially improving algorithm robustness through external validation.
levers.review: Early publication prioritizes scientific priority but delays reproducibility; parallel curation adds timeline pressure and risks incomplete de-identification if dataset changes are needed post-publication. External collaboration builds validation credibility but introduces coordination overhead and potential authorship disputes if the partner pursues independent analyses.

levers.name: Night-Shift Staffing Rotation and Coverage Continuity
levers.consequences: A rigid three-technician rotation covering 8 suites every night provides immediate incident response but locks in wage costs regardless of occupancy or absence. Conversely, a flexible on-call model with weekend-only overlap reduces fixed overhead but introduces delayed response times during peak event nights and increases burnout risk for the two full-time technicians, degrading annotation quality and inter-rater reliability over the first 18 months.
options: Hire a fourth part-time overnight technician on a split-shift schedule (21:00–02:00 and 02:00–07:00) to provide dedicated overlap coverage during the statistically busiest event hours, accepting the 20% wage increase in exchange for reduced response latency and annotation fatigue.

Maintain the original three-technician rotation but introduce a per-suite silent alarm escalation protocol that wakes the PI on call and a second technician from adjacent suites when motion or audio triggers exceed threshold, enabling coordinated response without a fourth body.

Stagger participant admissions so that no more than 6 of 8 suites are occupied simultaneously during the first 12 months, leaving capacity to absorb sick leave and vacation without hiring additional night staff, then reassess staffing ratios once operational baseline data validates safe suite-to-technician ratios.
levers.review: Three technicians covering 8 suites nightly creates fatigue-driven annotation errors that feed inter-rater disagreement; none of these options directly address seasonal or pandemic-driven absence surges that might force temporary closure.

levers.name: Dry-Electrode Headband Signal Quality Thresholding and False-Alarm Reduction
levers.consequences: Setting a permissive EEG signal-quality threshold on the nightly headband captures more candidate events but floods the annotation queue with motion artifact and respiration noise, requiring the technician and two independent scorers to dismiss dozens of non-events per week. Raising the threshold reduces false positives but risks missing low-amplitude confusional arousals and subtle leg-movement episodes, biasing the phenotype toward higher-amplitude events and introducing selection artifact into Aim 2 longitudinal characterization.
options: Deploy a rolling 48-hour sensor calibration phase for each participant using the first two headband nights to establish individual signal-quality baselines, then apply person-specific thresholds that account for electrode impedance drift and scalp conductivity variation, reducing false alarms by 30–40% without raising the absolute threshold.

Implement a two-tier annotation workflow: technician performs rapid triage flagging only high-confidence motor clusters in the first pass, then dual scorers review only flagged segments plus a random 15% sample of low-confidence segments, trading marginal sensitivity loss for a 50% reduction in dual-rater review time and fatigue.

Accept the false-alarm burden as a necessary cost of sensitivity during the pilot phase, logging all headband detections and final adjudication outcomes, then conduct a post-hoc analysis at month 12 to derive data-driven thresholds that maximize sensitivity and specificity against the accumulated ground truth of dual-scorer consensus events.
levers.review: Headband-derived false alarms drive annotation bottleneck and rater fatigue, but none of these options address inter-rater disagreement on borderline motor episodes when the true event morphology is genuinely ambiguous rather than artifact.

levers.name: Matched Control Recruitment Scope and Phenotyping Complexity
levers.consequences: Enrolling a 1:1 matched control group (15–20 controls alongside 50–70 parasomnias participants) provides definitive baseline sensor false-positive rates and normal nocturnal movement patterns for benchmarking event-triage tools, but doubles participant recruitment burden and adds ~8–10 weeks of facility occupancy during year one and two. A smaller control cohort (n=8–10) enrolled once and measured longitudinally reduces recruitment overhead but yields less statistical power for sensor-specificity claims and may not generalize across seasons or age subgroups.
options: Recruit and monitor 15 age-matched and sex-matched controls during year one in a dedicated 2-week intensive block, then retest a 50% subsample in year three to quantify seasonal variation in baseline arousal and movement; this front-loads control acquisition but yields robust phenotypic anchoring for Aim 2 analyses.

Enroll controls opportunistically from the University Hospital Bonn sleep clinic screening pool and the Deutsche Gesellschaft für Schlafforschung und Schlafmedizin network, recruiting 5–7 controls per quarter rather than in a block, spreading acquisition cost across 18 months but accepting lower matching fidelity and increased logistical complexity.

Defer formal matched control enrollment and instead use the first 10–12 parasomnias participants as their own pre-admission baseline: conduct one 3-night monitoring run before diagnostic confirmation, then enroll for treatment as usual; controls become unnecessary if cross-individual event-free nights sufficiently characterize sensor false-positive profiles, reducing recruitment pressure but weakening the generalizability of benchmarking data.
levers.review: Matched controls anchor event-triage benchmarking but require recruitment parity with patients, straining capacity during year one; none of these options distinguish between healthy young controls and age-representative normal sleepers, so specificity claims remain limited to the cohort composition.

levers.name: Data Retention Timeline and Regulatory Burden Trade-off
levers.consequences: Retaining raw sensor streams (EEG, video, audio, mattress, infrared) for the full 5-year standard research data archival period ensures full auditability and enables future reanalysis, but multiplies storage costs, privacy-compliance overhead, and legal liability if de-identification fails or a participant later objects to bedroom video retention. Purging raw video and audio after 12 months of phenotyping and event adjudication reduces privacy risk and storage burden by approximately 60% but forecloses future computer-vision or acoustic reanalysis and creates ambiguity about what "de-identified" video actually means under German data protection law.
options: Implement a tiered retention policy: keep raw EEG, contact-free sensors (mattress, infrared motion), and metadata indefinitely; delete all bedroom audio and video within 90 days of final event adjudication, storing only time-stamped motion-onset coordinates and expert-annotated event descriptions, minimizing privacy liability while preserving physiological reanalysis capability.

Secure explicit informed consent during recruitment specifically permitting 10-year video retention in a locked archive accessible only to the PI and independent ethics oversight; store video and audio on air-gapped encrypted drives in the university legal office, not on research NAS, creating institutional separation between clinical data and video materials and reducing hacking surface area.

Adopt a strict 12-month purge schedule for all raw sensory data (video, audio, mattress sensor waveforms) immediately following independent dual-score event adjudication and publication-related reanalysis, retaining only summary-level event timing, morphology codes, and EEG spectrograms, meeting German data minimization principles and reducing regulatory risk at the cost of forfeiting raw-signal reanalysis optionality.
levers.review: Video retention creates privacy and legal exposure proportional to duration, but deletion prevents future reanalysis; none of these options address the ambiguity of whether time-stamped motion coordinates alone constitute de-identification under GDPR if behavioral patterns are individually identifiable.

levers.name: Publication Sequencing and Funder Narrative Continuity
levers.consequences: Publishing the methods-validation and Aim 1 operational results first (month 18–20) establishes credibility with DFG and University of Bonn for year three funding but requires delaying high-impact Aim 2 phenotyping results until month 24–28, potentially ceding narrative momentum and allowing competitors to publish similar longitudinal characterizations. Publishing Aim 2 findings first (month 22–24) captures novelty but risks methods-validation criticism and may limit acceptance in top-tier journals if operational sustainability is not yet proven, weakening renewal justification.
options: Sequence publications as a dual-track strategy: submit the operational and inter-rater reliability methods paper to a sleep medicine journal at month 18, simultaneously developing a preprint of preliminary Aim 2 phenotype findings at month 20, allowing the phenotyping narrative to circulate while the peer-review process validates methods credibility, reducing journal competition pressure.

Prioritize a single high-visibility integrated publication at month 24 that binds methods validation (Aim 1) and preliminary longitudinal phenotyping (Aim 2) results in a unified narrative, leveraging the combined dataset and operational proof of concept to argue for continuation funding, accepting slower initial publication pace in exchange for coherence and impact.

Publish early and frequently: release operational and safety findings at month 12 as a short technical brief, then roll out Aim 2 phenotypic results in a series of three focused papers (one per parasomnia type) between months 20–28, building publication momentum and demonstrating sustained productivity to funder panels, but accepting fragmentation of the research narrative across multiple venues.
levers.review: Early publication establishes funder confidence but fragmented output dilutes narrative impact; deferring publication until Aim 2 solidifies scientific novelty but delays interim reporting that funders expect by month 18, risking conditional-year-three funding review.

levers.name: Equipment Lifecycle and Budget Flexibility Under Vendor Obsolescence
levers.consequences: Purchasing all sensor hardware and PSG equipment outright in year one (€450K budget) provides immediate availability and no recurring licensing fees but locks capital into gear with 3–5 year hardware lifecycles, risking obsolescence of dry-electrode headband technology or mattress sensors if competitors release materially superior designs by year two. Leasing or renting core PSG equipment spreads costs across years but introduces vendor lock-in, recurring annual fees (~€80–120K estimated), and potential service discontinuation if the rental provider exits the market.
options: Commit to purchasing the core PSG equipment and dry-electrode headbands outright in year one, then establish a technology-refresh contingency fund (€50–80K) in year two budgets to upgrade or replace underperforming sensors if benchmarking data (month 12) reveals false-alarm or signal-quality deficits, accepting some capital waste in exchange for flexibility and avoiding multi-year rental contracts.

Lease all non-permanent equipment (PSG amplifiers, dry-electrode headbands, camera and infrared hardware) on 24-month renewable agreements with the major manufacturers, treating equipment as operational expenses rather than capital, freeing budget for participant compensation and scoring labor but committing to €30K annual recurring costs and potential service interruptions.

Negotiate a volume-discount research partnership with the primary sensor vendors (Emotiv or comparable dry-EEG provider, Beddit or equivalent for mattress sensing) offering free or deeply discounted equipment in year one in exchange for publication acknowledgment and de-identified aggregate benchmarking data, deferring €100–150K in upfront equipment costs to year two conditional on partnership approval.
levers.review: Outright purchase locks capital and risk into hardware lifecycles; leasing spreads cost but creates vendor dependency; neither option hedges against fundamental sensor-technology disruption (e.g., transition from dry-electrode to textile-integrated sensing) without explicit contingency rebudgeting.

levers.name: Core Team Skill Composition and Operational Dependency Risk
levers.consequences: Hiring two postdoctoral researchers with PhDs in sleep neurophysiology and computational neuroscience (per the current staffing plan) ensures deep domain expertise for algorithm development and Aim 3 triage-tool benchmarking, but both roles are typically 2–3 year appointments, creating turnover risk and knowledge loss if either postdoc departs before month 18. Alternatively, hiring a single mid-career research scientist (MSc-level, 5+ years sleep lab experience) paired with a junior computational analyst reduces domain depth and limits Aim 3 algorithm sophistication but provides stability and lower salary drag, freeing €80–120K for participant compensation or technician support over three years.
options: Recruit the two postdoctoral researchers as planned, but negotiate explicit co-mentorship and cross-training protocols: the sleep neurophysiology postdoc mentors one research technician in semi-automated event detection during months 6–12, and the computational postdoc documents all algorithm development in a shared GitHub repository with comprehensive annotations, ensuring operational continuity if either postdoc departs by year three.

Hire a single tenured or indefinite-contract research scientist (sleep neurophysiology background, age 40–55) alongside one full-time junior data analyst, accepting reduced cutting-edge algorithmic ambition for Aim 3 but gaining institutional memory, willingness to supervise technicians long-term, and lower turnover risk, reallocating €50K from salaries to technician peer-support training and participant incentives.

Maintain the two-postdoc structure but add a commitment to co-author agreements requiring collaborative publication during the second postdoc's final year and a mandatory 3-month knowledge-transition period before departure; simultaneously hire a third part-time graduate-student research assistant (10 h/wk) to shadow both postdocs and build algorithmic literacy, creating a tiered skill buffer against mid-career departures.
levers.review: Two postdocs provide algorithmic depth but 2–3 year appointments create continuity risk; none of these options directly address recruitment difficulty for specialized postdoctoral talent in smaller research markets like Bonn, potentially extending hiring timelines by 2–4 months and delaying project start.

levers.name: Exclusion Criteria Adjudication and Recruitment Velocity Trade-off
levers.consequences: Strict pre-admission adjudication (specialist clinical interview, bed-partner collateral, prior polysomnography, structured exclusion checklist) minimizes misdiagnosis and excludes mimics (nocturnal epilepsy, uncontrolled apnea, psychiatric instability) but requires 4–6 weeks of vetting per referral, reducing recruitment velocity to 4–6 participants per quarter and risking enrollment shortfall during year one if referral channels are slow to establish. Streamlined screening (telephone symptom checklist plus one polysomnography session) accelerates admission to 10–12 participants per quarter but risks enrolling atypical cases (ambiguous epilepsy-parasomnia overlap, subclinical apnea) that distort phenotyping and increase false-event rates.
options: Implement a two-stage filtering process: rapid telephone triage (30 min) by a trained sleep coordinator eliminates obvious exclusions (untreated epilepsy, active substance use), then schedule in-person PI interview and prior polysomnography review only for screened-positive candidates, reducing vetting time to 2–3 weeks and achieving 8–10 quarterly admissions without loosening exclusion precision.

Establish a standing weekly "diagnostic case conference" with the PI, clinical psychologist, and a collaborating neurologist from the University Hospital Bonn epilepsy service, where borderline referrals (possible nocturnal seizures, RBD-parasomnia overlap) are discussed before rejection, creating a second-opinion buffer that converts 15–20% of otherwise-excluded cases into admitted participants with documented adjudication rationale.

Maintain strict pre-admission criteria (specialist interview, collateral, prior PSG, structured checklist) and use slow initial recruitment to validate the diagnostic pipeline thoroughly, accepting lower year-one enrollment (12–15 participants) but building operational confidence and reducing mid-study protocol deviations, then scale recruitment aggressively in year two once the vetting process is proven robust.
levers.review: Strict pre-admission screening ensures phenotypic homogeneity but delays recruitment; rapid screening accelerates admissions but introduces diagnostic ambiguity; none of these options address the limited availability of prior polysomnography in referred cases, which may force real-time diagnostic screening polysomnography during the facility stay rather than pre-admission.

Plan:
Establish a 3-year residential longitudinal research unit in Bonn, Germany, for the study of adult NREM parasomnias — sleepwalking, confusional arousals, and sleep terrors — with a secondary exploratory arm for REM sleep behavior disorder under a separate protocol with dedicated neurologic screening, reflecting RBD's distinct clinical trajectory per current AASM guidance. The facility is affiliated with University Hospital Bonn's Department of Epileptology, leveraging its existing long-term video-EEG monitoring culture, and addresses a specific methodological gap: traditional single-night polysomnography rarely captures infrequent parasomnia events, while outpatient actigraphy lacks physiological resolution. The unit houses 8 active sleep suites at launch in a converted residential property in a quiet Bonn neighborhood, renovated for safety (padded corridor edges, restricted-opening windows, silent exterior door alarms, fire safety, acoustic treatment, network cabling, accessibility modifications) while preserving a domestic feel — if the environment is too clinical, naturalistic behavior is suppressed. Physical capacity exists for 12 suites, but expansion is deferred until the pilot proves acceptable data quality, manageable false alarm rates, safe staffing ratios, and usable annotation throughput. Sensing uses a tiered acquisition model: nightly low-burden monitoring via dry-electrode EEG headbands, contact-free mattress sensors, unobtrusively mounted infrared cameras, ambient microphones, and environmental sensors; scheduled enhanced nights with fuller PSG montage including standard scalp EEG, EOG, chin EMG, and leg EMG on the first night, one mid-stay night, and the final night per participant; and escalation nights deploying full PSG after technician-flagged events to capture recurrence at clinical-grade resolution. All streams are time-synchronized and stored in EEG-BIDS-compatible format on a local NAS with nightly encrypted backup to university storage, annotated in real time by the night technician and later scored by two independent raters using AASM criteria with inter-rater reliability reported. Public data sharing is limited to de-identified physiological and sensor data under data use agreements — bedroom video carries severe privacy constraints and is not deposited in public repositories. The scientific program has three explicit aims: Aim 1, establish and operationally validate the residential capture model as safe, ethics-approved, and sustainable; Aim 2, characterize within-person and between-person parasomnia patterns longitudinally, including episode frequency, morphology, triggers, and temporal clustering; Aim 3, develop and benchmark semi-automated event-triage tools that rank probable parasomnia episodes and reduce manual review burden, evaluated against dual human scorer agreement rather than promising autonomous diagnosis.

Participant recruitment targets adults aged 18–65 with NREM parasomnia confirmed through a structured pre-admission pathway: specialist clinical interview, collateral history from bed partner or household member where available, prior or screening polysomnography, and a structured exclusion checklist adjudicated by the PI. Explicit exclusions are nocturnal epilepsy or suspected epilepsy mimics, untreated obstructive sleep apnea, active major substance use disorder, severe psychiatric instability, and wandering or injury risk beyond facility capability. Recruitment channels are the University Hospital Bonn sleep clinic, regional neurologist referrals, and the Deutsche Gesellschaft für Schlafforschung und Schlafmedizin network, with per-night compensation of €80 plus meals. A matched control group provides baseline nocturnal movement, arousal patterns, and false-positive sensor activity under identical residential monitoring conditions, enabling benchmarking of the event-triage tools against normal nocturnal behavior. Event-yield planning assumes that based on the inclusion criterion of at least 2 self-reported episodes per month, approximately 70–80% of admitted participants will produce at least one captured and adjudicated event during a 2–8 week stay; stays may be extended up to 2 additional weeks for participants with zero captured events after the initial period, capped at 10 weeks total, with a protocol ceiling of 20% unproductive admissions before triggering a recruitment-criteria review. The core team is 9 people: a PI who is a board-certified sleep medicine physician, 2 postdoctoral researchers in sleep neurophysiology and computational neuroscience respectively, 3 research technicians rotating night shifts to ensure safe coverage of 8 active suites with adequate margin for event response and annotation, a clinical psychologist specializing in sleep disorders, a data engineer managing the sensor pipeline, and a study coordinator handling recruitment, consent, scheduling, and ethics compliance.

Budget is €3.8 million over 3 years, gated: €1.8M year one covering property lease and renovation at approximately €750K, equipment at approximately €450K, staff hiring accounting for German social insurance contributions and actual overnight coverage, ethics approval, and a pilot cohort of 15–20 participants; €1.2M year two covering full operations with 30–35 participants, the enhanced-night PSG program, first publications, and event-triage algorithm development; €800K year three conditional on demonstrable progress by month 24. Personnel costs are approximately €2M over three years and remaining funds cover participant compensation, independent scoring time, data storage and retention, regulatory and legal work, and contingency. Funding sources are DFG research grant and University of Bonn internal research funding as the primary pillars, with a pharmaceutical industry partnership as optional upside rather than a feasibility requirement — if secured, the academic team retains full publication rights with the pharma partner receiving a 30-day pre-publication comment window only. Success criteria at 36 months: safe residential monitoring operations sustained for at least 24 months, enrollment of 50–70 NREM parasomnia participants plus matched controls, capture of a prespecified minimum number of independently adjudicated parasomnia events sufficient for Aim 2 phenotyping analysis, 2–3 peer-reviewed publications in sleep medicine journals covering methods validation and longitudinal characterization, a benchmarked semi-automated event-triage model with reported sensitivity, specificity, and agreement against dual human scoring, de-identified physiological dataset deposited in a recognized repository, and a submitted phase-two grant proposal for expansion and intervention studies. Failure triggers: if by month 18 the facility has enrolled fewer than 25 participants or captured fewer than 40 adjudicated events, the program undergoes external review. Governance is a 3-member external scientific advisory board reviewing progress every 6 months, with the PI holding operational authority and budget reallocations above €50K requiring board approval.
